title: Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis: renal interstitium
vignette: A 47-year-old man is treated for bacterial sinusitis with ampicillin. A week later he comes to the emergency department with fever and a skin rash. He also reports low urine output. Temperature is 37.5 C (99.5 F), blood pressure is 123/71 mm Hg, and pulse is 88/min. Physical examination shows a diffuse maculopapular rash. Serum creatinine level is 2.4 mg/dL, and urine sediment microscopy reveals 3-4 red blood cells/hpf, 5-10 white blood cells/hpf, and 3-5 eosinophils/hpf. The pathologic process affecting this patient's kidneys most likely involves which of the following structures?

clues.text: treated for bacterial sinusitis with ampicillin
clues.note: A recent new drug - especially a beta-lactam (ampicillin) - is the classic trigger of acute interstitial nephritis (AIN), typically 1-3 weeks after starting the drug.
Fever + rash + acute kidney injury after a new drug is the hypersensitivity triad of AIN.
Acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.4 / normal 0.6-1.2 mg/dL) after a new drug, with pyuria/eosinophiluria, points to AIN affecting the interstitium/tubules.
Urinary EOSINOPHILS (eosinophiluria) with white cells strongly suggest an allergic/hypersensitivity interstitial process - AIN - rather than glomerular disease.

whatMatters: Fever + maculopapular rash + acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.4) + pyuria with EOSINOPHILURIA, 1-2 weeks after starting a beta-lactam (ampicillin) = drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis (AIN). The hypersensitivity inflammation primarily involves the RENAL INTERSTITIUM (with edema and leukocyte infiltration). Answer C.
strategy: Recognize the AIN triad (fever, rash, AKI) + eosinophiluria after a culprit drug, then localize: AIN = inflammation of the renal INTERSTITIUM (and tubules), not glomeruli. Answer C. Reject other renal compartments: calyces/ureters (stones), glomeruli (nephritic disease with dysmorphic RBCs/casts), renal papillae (papillary necrosis), and small arterioles (hypertensive/diabetic).

eliminations.label: Calyces and ureters - nephrolithiasis
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: obstruction of the collecting system (stones) can cause hematuria and AKI. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: nephrolithiasis causes flank pain, not fever/rash/eosinophiluria. ✅ Correct if: obstructing stone with hydronephrosis and colicky flank pain.

eliminations.label: Glomeruli - nephritic disease, your pick
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: glomerular injury (e.g., poststreptococcal GN) causes AKI. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: glomerular disease shows dysmorphic RBCs and/or RBC casts - here the picture (rash, fever, eosinophiluria after a drug) is interstitial, not glomerular. ✅ Correct if: nephritic syndrome with dysmorphic RBCs/RBC casts.

eliminations.label: Renal papillae - papillary necrosis
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: papillary necrosis (sickle cell, diabetes, analgesic nephropathy, severe pyelonephritis) causes hematuria/sterile pyuria. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it doesn't cause a drug-hypersensitivity rash/eosinophiluria. ✅ Correct if: gross hematuria with sloughed papillae in a predisposed patient.

eliminations.label: Small renal arterioles - hypertensive/diabetic nephropathy
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: arteriolar damage in hypertension or diabetes. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: those cause proteinuria/chronic changes, not acute pyuria with eosinophils after a drug. ✅ Correct if: hypertensive/diabetic nephropathy (proteinuria).

reasoning: A new drug (ampicillin, a beta-lactam) 1-2 weeks earlier + fever + rash + AKI = acute interstitial nephritis
Urine shows pyuria with EOSINOPHILS (eosinophiluria), an allergic/interstitial pattern
AIN is a hypersensitivity inflammation of the renal interstitium and tubules
mechanism: Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is a hypersensitivity reaction (IgE-mediated type I or cell-mediated type IV) most commonly triggered by drugs - classically beta-lactam antibiotics, but also sulfonamides, rifampin, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, and diuretics - typically 1-3 weeks after exposure. It presents with fever, maculopapular rash, and acute kidney injury (elevated creatinine, oliguria), often with peripheral eosinophilia and eosinophiluria, plus pyuria, white cell casts, and mild hematuria. The inflammation primarily involves the RENAL INTERSTITIUM, causing interstitial edema and a leukocyte infiltrate (lymphocytes, macrophages, eosinophils) with tubulitis and sometimes granulomas; the glomeruli and vessels are relatively spared. Symptoms usually resolve on stopping the offending drug. The distractors localize to the collecting system (stones), glomeruli (nephritic disease with dysmorphic RBCs/casts), renal papillae (papillary necrosis), and arterioles (hypertensive/diabetic nephropathy).

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Renal > acute interstitial nephritis: drug hypersensitivity (beta-lactams, NSAIDs, PPIs, sulfa, rifampin, diuretics); fever/rash/AKI + eosinophiluria; interstitial inflammation.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: Read the triad (fever, rash, AKI) + eosinophiluria after a new drug as AIN, then localize to the interstitium.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on interstitium vs glomerulus, eosinophiluria, pyuria, maculopapular, or hypersensitivity type I/IV? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Glomeruli (your pick) would show dysmorphic RBCs/RBC casts (nephritic), not eosinophiluria; stones (calyces/ureters), papillary necrosis, and arteriolar disease each miss the drug-allergy picture.

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: new drug (beta-lactam) + fever + rash + AKI + eosinophiluria = acute interstitial nephritis (renal interstitium); stop the drug.

memoryHook: New drug, then fever + rash + failing kidneys with EOSINOPHILS in the urine: the interstitium is inflamed - stop the drug.
